findings.title: Negative offset slicing crashes Django querysets
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result special-cases `cursor.offset < 0` and slices the queryset directly with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` can be negative. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level', but this is incorrect — any request using `enable_advanced_features=True` (now wired up in organization_auditlogs.py) with a crafted cursor containing a negative offset will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 to the client.

findings.title: Inconsistent/incomplete clamping of negative offsets in BasePaginator
findings.body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps the offset to be non-negative for the forward-paging branch; for `cursor.is_prev=True` the raw (potentially negative) `offset` is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Since `Cursor.offset` can be set to a negative integer via `Cursor.from_string` (e.g. a crafted `cursor` query param like `0:-5:1`), this reaches the ORM with a negative slice bound and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported`, affecting every endpoint using `BasePaginator`/`DateTimePaginator`/`Paginator`, not just the new optimized paginator.

findings.title: Misleading comment about negative offset support with no validation added
findings.body: The added comment claims negative offsets are an intentional 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions', but no validation was added to `Cursor.__init__` or `Cursor.from_string` to bound the offset, and downstream consumers (BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator) do not safely handle negative offsets against Django querysets (see other findings). This comment documents behavior that is not actually safe or supported, which will mislead future maintainers.

findings.title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses `organization_context.member.has_global_access` unconditionally. For a superuser who is not an actual member of the organization, `organization_context.member` can be `None`, and Python's `or` still evaluates/accesses `.has_global_access` on the right-hand side only if the left side is falsy — but even for non-superuser staff with no org membership this attribute access will raise `AttributeError` instead of returning a controlled 403/400, turning what should be a permission check into an unhandled 500 error.

findings.title: Eviction can silently remove the segment's root span without updating the has-root-span flag
findings.body: When `span_count > 1000`, `zpopmin` removes the lowest-scored members from `set_key`, where the score is `end_timestamp_precise`. There is no protection to keep the span whose `span_id` equals the segment key (the root/segment span) from being evicted. Meanwhile `has_root_span_key` is set independently as a separate boolean flag and is not affected by eviction. If the actual root span payload is evicted, `flush_segments` in buffer.py (which derives `is_segment` by comparing each remaining payload's `span_id` to the segment key) will never find a span with `is_segment=True`, even though the segment is still flushed as if it has a root span. This produces inconsistent/incorrect output for consumers relying on the root span marker.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new per-insert eviction logic
findings.body: This PR's stated purpose is 'eviction during insert' via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment exceeds 1000 spans, but no test in tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., inserting >1000 spans into one segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 remain, or that a root span is preserved). The core new behavior introduced by this PR is therefore untested.

findings.title: max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code with a mismatched hardcoded limit in Lua
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the only code that used to enforce it (the span-count check in `_load_segment_data` that logged `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and dropped oversized segments) has been removed. The actual limit enforcement moved into `add-buffer.lua` as a hardcoded `1000` constant, which is not driven by `self.max_segment_spans` at all. This leaves a misleading, unused constructor parameter (callers may believe they can tune this value, but it no longer has any effect) and a silent off-by-one mismatch (1001 vs 1000) between the old config default and the new hardcoded behavior.

findings.title: Loss of observability for oversized segments after moving limit enforcement into Redis
findings.body: Previously, segments exceeding `max_segment_spans` were fully dropped with an `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` error metric and log line, giving operators visibility into data loss. That code path was removed in this diff. The replacement eviction logic in add-buffer.lua silently pops the lowest-scored members with no metric or log emitted, so operators lose visibility into how often/how much span data is being evicted due to the 1000-span cap.

findings.title: Redirect depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 without updated justification
findings.body: The loop bound for resolving redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted entirely rather than updated. This is a behavioral change (traces with redirect/segment depth between 1000 and 10000 will now fail to join correctly) with no comment or changelog explaining why the threshold was lowered or whether it's intentionally aligned with the new 1000-span cap.

findings.title: No tests added for the new OptimizedCursorPaginator
findings.body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class (and the `enable_advanced_features`/negative-offset code path it introduces) has no corresponding unit tests anywhere in the diff, despite being wired into a user-facing endpoint (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) and gated by a permission check that itself has a bug (see organization_auditlogs.py finding). Given this class diverges from BasePaginator's slicing behavior specifically around boundary conditions, it should have dedicated tests, including for negative-offset inputs that currently crash.
